title: Introduction to Quarto
text:
File Management
As boring as it sounds, file management is arguably one of the most important skills a data scientist should have. The reproducibility of a project depends just as much on the way in which the project was stored as the computing tools used. While using R and Quarto make an important step in creating a reproducible analysis, there are other pieces that are arguably just as important—such as file management.
Believe it or not, your computer has multiple locations** where files can be stored. There has been a bit of a generational shift as computers have evolved: the “file system” metaphor itself is outdated because no one uses physical files anymore.
[This article]((https://futurism.com/the-byte/gen-z-kids-file-systems) makes the argument that with modern search capabilities, most people use their computers as a laundry hamper instead of as a nice, organized filing cabinet. However, the laundry hamper approach doesn’t play nicely with working in R and creating Quarto documents.
A good programmer will store files according to the Project TIER protocol. More specifically, you will have:

a “Stat 250” folder in your Documents folder, containing all your materials associated with STAT 250
a sub-folder for each week (e.g., Week 1, Week 2)
separate folders within each week for each assignment (e.g., Practice Activity, Lab)

Variables, files, code chunks, and other objects are named appropriately and add to the scripts readability.

title: Continuous Random Variables
text:
1 Continuous Random Variable
Definition: Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a set. Let \(a\) and \(b\) be two arbitrary elements in \(\mathcal{S}\). If there are a finite number of elements between \(a\) and \(b\), \(\mathcal{S}\) is countable. Otherwise, \(\mathcal{S}\) is uncountable.
Example: Let \(\mathcal{C} = \{ 1, 2, 3, \dots \}\). If we choose any two elements in \(\mathcal{C}\), there are a finite number of elements between them. Therefore, \(\mathcal{C}\) is a countable set.
Example: Let \(\mathcal{U} = (0, 1)\), the set of all real numbers between 0 and 1 exclusive. Let us consider two elements 0.2 and 0.3 in \(\mathcal{U}\). There are infinitely many elements between the two elements. Therefore, \(\mathcal{U}\) is an uncountable set.
Definition: Let \(X\) be a random variable and \(\mathcal{S}_X\) be the support of \(X\). If \(\mathcal{S}_X\) is countable (or countably infinite), \(X\) is a discrete random variable. If \(\mathcal{S}_X\) is uncountable, then \(X\) is a continuous random variable.
In the previous lecture, we focused on discrete random variables. If \(X\) is a discrete random variable with \(\mathcal{S}_X\), we use a probability mass function (PMF) to represent its probability model. In this lecture, we focus on continuous random variables. If \(X\) is a continuous random variable with \(\mathcal{S}_X\), we need to use calculus (integration) for probability calculation.

title: Continuous Random Variables
text:
2 Probability Density Function
Definition: Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable and \(\mathcal{S}_X\) be the support of \(X\). We say \(f_X\): \(\mathcal{S}_X \rightarrow \mathcal{R}\) is a probability density function (or PDF) if it satisfies the following two conditions:

\(f_X(x) \ge 0\) for any \(x \in \mathcal{S}_X\)
\(\int_{\mathcal{S}_X} f_X(x) \, dx = 1\)

When we have a continuous random variable, we use the integration \(\int\) instead of the summation \(\sum\).
Example: Let \(T\) be the time to finish a 2-hour exam. Its support is \(\mathcal{S}_T = (0, 2)\), all real numbers between 0 and 2. Assume the PDF of \(T\) is given by
\[
f_T(t) = \frac{3}{8} \, t^2 \, , \,\,\, 0 < t < 2 \, .
\tag{1}\]
It is a legitimate PDF as it satisfies the two conditions:

\(\frac{3}{8} \, t^2 \ge 0\) for \(0 < t < 2\)
\(\int_0^2 \frac{3}{8} \, t^2 \, dt = 1\).

The PDF is graphically shown below.









We do not interpret \(f_T(t)\) as the probability of \(T = t\). In fact, the probability of \(T = t\) is zero. Instead, we can calculate the probability of \(t_1 \le T \le t_2\). For example, the probability that a student finishes the exam after 1 hour is
\(P(1 < T < 2) =\)






NoteAnswer





\[
P(1 < T < 2) = \int_1^2 f_T(t) \, dt = \int_1^2 \frac{3}{8} \, t^2 \, dt = 0.875 \, .
\]



The probability that a student finishes the exam before 1 hour is
\(P(0 < T < 1) =\)






NoteAnswer





\[
P(0 < T < 1) = \int_0^1 f_T(t) \, dt = \int_0^1 \frac{3}{8} \, t^2 \, dt = 0.125 \, .
\]



Note: The value of \(f_T(t)\) is called the density of \(T = t\). It has a theoretical interpretation rather than a practical interpretation. For example,
\[
\frac{f_T(1.5)}{f_T(0.5)} = \frac{(1.5)^2}{(0.5)^2} = 9 \, ,
\]
and it is theoretically interpreted as \(T = 1.5\) is 9 times more plausible outcome than \(T = 0.5\). Loosely speaking, if 100 students needed about 0.5 hours to finish the exam, about we expect th 900 students would need about 1.5 hours.

title: Continuous Random Variables
text:
3 Expectation
Definition: The expectation of a continuous random variable \(X\) is defined as
\[
E(X) = \int_{\mathcal{S}_X} x \cdot f_X(x) \, dx \, .
\]
It is also called the average, mean, and expected value of \(X\).
In some sense, it is the weighted average of all values in \(\mathcal{S}_X\) and each value in \(\mathcal{S}_X\) is weighted by the density \(f_X(x)\). Since \(\mathcal{S}_X\) is uncountable, we sum over \(\mathcal{S}_X\) using the integration \(\int\) instead of the summation \(\sum\).
Example: In the previous example, the expected time to finish the exam is
\(E(X) =\)






NoteAnswer





\[
E(X) = \int_{\mathcal{S}_T} t \cdot f_T(t) \, dt = \int_0^2 t \cdot \frac{3}{8} \, t^2 \, dt = 1.5 \, .
\]



In other words, students need 1.5 hours to finish the exam on average. (It does not imply that most students need 1.5 hours.)

title: Continuous Random Variables
text:
4 Variance
Definition: The variance of a continuous random variable \(X\) is defined as
\[
V(X) = \int_{\mathcal{S}_X} [x - E(X)]^2 \cdot f_X(x) \, dx \, .
\]
Definition: The standard deviation of \(X\) is defined as \(\sqrt{V(X)}\).
Example: In the previous example, the variance of \(T\) is
\(V(T) =\)






NoteAnswer





\[
V(T) = \int_0^2 (t - 1.5)^2 \cdot \frac{3}{8} \, t^2 \, dt = 0.15 \, ,
\]



and the standard deviation of \(T\) is \(\sqrt{0.15} = 0.387\).

title: Continuous Random Variables
text:
5 Parametric Models
A PDF can serve as a probability model for a continuous variable, and it can be more flexible by attaching a model parameter. Let \(T\) be the time to finish a 2-hour exam, and consider the following PDF:
\[
f_T(t) = \frac{1}{2^{\theta + 1}} \, (\theta + 1) \, t^\theta \, , \,\,\, 0 < t < 2
\tag{2}\]
where \(\theta > 1\) is a model parameter (fixed). Note that the PDF in Equation 1 is a special case of the PDF in Equation 2 when \(\theta = 2\). The PDF in Equation 2 is flexible by choosing the value of \(\theta\). The below figure demonstrates the shapes of \(f_T\) at \(\theta = 1\), \(\theta = 2\), and \(\theta = 4\).









There are many parametric probability models that statisticians use depending on the distribution of data to be observed. The following subsections introduce three popular parametric models known as the exponential distribution, uniform distribution, and normal distribution.

5.1 Exponential Distribution
Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable where \(\mathcal{S}_X = (0, \infty)\). We say \(X\) follows an exponential distribution with a parameter \(\theta > 0\) when its PDF is given by
\[
f_X(x) = \frac{1}{\theta} \, e^{-\frac{x}{\theta}} \, , \,\,\, 0 < x < \infty \, .
\]
In this case, we write \(X \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\theta)\). The below figure shows the exponential distributions at \(\theta = 1\), \(\theta = 2\), and \(\theta = 5\).









Example: Suppose you call customer service. Let \(X\) be the waiting time (minutes) until someone answers your call. Assume \(X \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\theta)\) with \(\theta = 5\). Under this assumption, the probability model for \(X\) is represented by the PDF
\[
f_X(x) = \frac{1}{5} \, e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \, , \,\,\, 0 < x < \infty \, . \notag
\]
The probability that the waiting time is at most 1 minute is






NoteAnswer





\[
P(X \le 1) = \int_0^1 \frac{1}{5} \, e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \, dx = 0.1813 \, .
\]



It can be calculated by the \(\texttt{pexp}\) function as follows.








The probability that the waiting time is longer than 1 minute is






NoteAnswer





\[
P(X > 1) = 1 - P(X \le 1) = 1 - 0.1813 = 0.8187 \, .
\]











When \(X \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\theta)\), the probability \(P(X \le x)\) or \(P(X < x)\) can be calculated by \(\texttt{pexp}( x, 1 / \theta )\), and the probability \(P(X > x)\) or \(P(X \ge x)\) can be calculated by \(1 - \texttt{pexp}( x, 1 / \theta)\).
By the definition of expectation and of variance,
\[ \begin{aligned}
E(X) & = \int_{\mathcal{S}_X} x \cdot f_X(x) \, dx \\
& = \int_0^\infty x \cdot \frac{1}{5} \, e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \, dx \\
& = 5 \,
\end{aligned}\]
and
\[\begin{aligned}
V(X) & = \int_{\mathcal{S}_X} [x - E(X)]^2 \cdot f_X(x) \, dx \\
& = \int_0^\infty (x - 5)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{5} \, e^{-\frac{x}{5}} \, dx \\
& = 25 \, .
\end{aligned}\]
The above integration can be done by the integration by parts or by the \(\texttt{integrate}\) function in R as follows.








Note: When \(X \sim \mathrm{Exp}(\theta)\), for any choice of \(\theta  > 0\), it can be shown that the expectation and variance of \(X\) are as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(X) & = \int_0^\infty x \cdot \frac{1}{\theta} \, e^{-\frac{x}{\theta}} \, dx = \theta \, , \\
V(X) & = \int_0^\infty (x - \theta)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{\theta} \, e^{-\frac{x}{\theta}} \, dx = \theta^2 \, .
\end{aligned}
\]


5.2 Uniform Distribution
Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable where \(\mathcal{S}_X = (\theta_1, \theta_2)\) for some \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) such that \(-\infty < \theta_1 < \theta_2 < \infty\). We say \(X\) follows a uniform distribution with parameters \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) when its PDF is given by
\[
f_X(x) = \frac{1}{\theta_2 - \theta_1} \, , \,\,\, \theta_1 < x < \theta_2 \, .
\]
In this case, we write \(X \sim \mathrm{Unif}(\theta_1, \theta_2)\). The below figure shows the uniform distribution at some \(\theta_1\) (lower bound) and \(\theta_2\) (upper bound).









Example: Suppose a bus arrives at a bus stop every 10 minutes. The bus schedule is unknown to you, and you go to the bus stop at a random time. Let \(X\) be the waiting time (minutes) until the bus arrives. In this case, it is reasonable to assume \(X \sim \mathrm{Unif}(\theta_1, \theta_2)\) where \(\theta_1 = 0\) and \(\theta_2 = 10\). Under this assumption, the probability model for \(X\) is represented by the PDF
\[ f_X(x) = \frac{1}{10 - 0} \, , \,\,\, 0 < x < 10 \, . \notag \]
The probability that the waiting time is at most 1 minute is






NoteAnswer





\[
P(X \le 1) = \int_0^1 \frac{1}{10} \, dx = 0.1 \, ,
\]



and the probability that the waiting time is at least 1 minute is






NoteAnswer





\[
P(X \ge 1) = \int_1^{10} \frac{1}{10} \, dx = 0.9 \, .
\]



The expectation and variance of \(X\) are






NoteAnswer





\[
\begin{aligned}
E(X) & = \int_{\mathcal{S}_X} x \cdot f_X(x) \, dx = \int_0^{10} x \cdot \frac{1}{10} \, dx = 5 \, , \\
V(X) & = \int_{\mathcal{S}_X} [x - E(X)]^2 \cdot f_X(x) \, dx = \int_0^{10} (x - 5)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{10} \, dx = 8.3333 \, .
\end{aligned}
\]



Note: When \(X \sim \mathrm{Unif}(\theta_1, \theta_2)\), for any choice of \(-\infty < \theta_1 < \theta_2 < \infty\), it can be shown that the expectation and variance of \(X\) are as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(X) & = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} x \cdot \frac{1}{\theta_2 - \theta_1} \, dx = \frac{\theta_1 + \theta_2}{2} \, , \\
V(X) & = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \left(x - \frac{\theta_1 + \theta_2}{2} \right)^2 \cdot \frac{1}{\theta_2 - \theta_1} \, dx = \frac{(\theta_2 - \theta_1)^2}{12} \, .
\end{aligned}
\]
The expectation of \(X\) is the midpoint of the lower bound \(\theta_1\) and the upper bound \(\theta_2\) of the support, and the variance of \(X\) increases as the distance between \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) increases.


5.3 Normal Distribution
Let \(X\) be a continuous random variable where \(\mathcal{S}_X = (-\infty, \infty)\). We say \(X\) follows a normal distribution (or Gaussian distribution) with parameters \(-\infty< \mu < \infty\) and \(\sigma > 0\) when its PDF is given by
\[
f_X(x) = \frac{1}{ \sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2} } \, e^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}} \, , \,\,\, -\infty < x < \infty \, .
\]
In this case, we write \(X \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma)\). The below figure shows the two normal distributions at \((\mu, \sigma) = (65, 5)\) and \((\mu, \sigma) = (70, 4)\).









Example: Let \(X\) be the height (inches) of adult women. Assume \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma)\) where \(\mu = 65\) and \(\sigma = 5\). The PDF of \(X\) is given by
\[
f_X(x) = \frac{1}{ \sqrt{2 \pi (5)^2} } \, e^{-\frac{(x - 65)^2}{2(5)^2}} \, , \,\,\, -\infty < x < \infty \, .
\]
Under this assumption, the probability that a woman is 68 inches or shorter is
\[
P(X \le 68) = \int_{-\infty}^{68} f_X(x) \, dx = \int_{-\infty}^{68} \frac{1}{ \sqrt{2 \pi (5)^2} } \, e^{-\frac{(x - 65)^2}{2(5)^2}} \, dx = 0.726 \, .
\]
The above probability calculation can be done by the \(\texttt{pnorm}\) function as follows.








Given this probability calculation, the probability that a woman is taller than 68 inches is \(P(X > 68) = 1 - P(X \le 68) = 0.274\).








When \(X \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma)\), the probability \(P(X \le x)\) or \(P(X < x)\) can be calculated by \(\texttt{pnorm}( x, \mu, \sigma )\), and the probability \(P(X > x)\) or \(P(X \ge x)\) can be calculated by \(1 - \texttt{pnorm}( x, \mu, \sigma )\).
The expectation and variance of \(X\) are
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(X) & = \int_{\mathcal{S}_X} x \cdot f_X(x) \, dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{x}{ \sqrt{2 \pi (5)^2} } \, e^{-\frac{(x - 65)^2}{2(5)^2}} \, dx = 65 \, , \\
V(X) & = \int_{\mathcal{S}_X} [x - E(X)]^2 \cdot f_X(x) \, dx = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(x - 65)^2}{ \sqrt{2 \pi (5)^2} } \, e^{-\frac{(x - 65)^2}{2(5)^2}} \, dx = 25 \, .
\end{aligned}
\]
Note: When \(X \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma)\), for any choice of \(-\infty < \mu < \infty\) and \(\sigma > 0\), it can be shown that the expectation and variance of \(X\) are as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(X) & = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{x}{ \sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2} } \, e^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}} \, dx = \mu \, , \\
V(X) & = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{(x - \mu)^2}{ \sqrt{2 \pi \sigma^2} } \, e^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}} \, dx = \sigma^2 \, .
\end{aligned}
\]
Because of the above properties, the model parameter \(\mu\) is referred to as the model expectation (model mean, model average, or model expected value), and the model parameter \(\sigma\) is referred to as the model standard deviation. (\(\sigma^2\) is referred to as the model variance.)
Definition: When \(X \sim \mathrm{N}( \mu, \sigma )\) where \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 1\), we say \(X\) follows the standard normal distribution.

text:
1 Bayes’ Theorem
Some events are observable, while some are not. For example, we can observe whether a lie detector indicates positive or negative, but we never know whether the subject lied or not. Suppose a criminal suspect is under investigation. Let \(L\) denote the event that the suspect lies (unknown) and \(D\) denote the event that the lie detector indicates a lie (observable). Assume the following.

If a suspect lies, the lie detector indicates that it is a lie with a probability of 0.8.
If a suspect tells truth, the lie detector indicates that it is a lie with a probability of 0.05.
A suspects lies with a probability of 0.9.

Given the notations \(L\) and \(D\), the above assumptions can be expressed as

\(P(D \mid L) = 0.8\),
\(P(D \mid L^c) = 0.05\), and
\(P(L) = 0.9\).

If the investigator observes a lie signal, what is the probability that the suspect lied? In other words, what is \(P(L \mid D)\)?

Theorem: For two events \(A\) and \(B\), the conditional probability of \(B\) given \(A\) is
\[P(B \mid A) = \frac{ P(A \mid B)\cdot P(B) }{ P(A) }\]
provided that \(P(A) > 0\). This statement is known as the Bayes’ Theorem.
Recall: Since \(B\) and \(B^c\) are a partition of any sample space,
\[P(A) = P(A \mid B) \cdot P(B) + P(A \mid B^c) \cdot P(B^c) \, . \] Therefore, the Bayes’ Theorem can be also written as
\[P(B \mid A) = \frac{ P(A \mid B) \cdot P(B) }{ P(A \mid B) \cdot P(B) + P(A \mid B^c) \cdot P(B^c) } \, . \tag{1}\]
Recall: \(P(E^c) = 1 - P(E)\) for any event \(E\).
This property holds for a conditional probability. In other words, \(P(E^c \mid C) = 1 - P(E \mid C)\) for any possible condition \(C\).
Therefore, Equation 1 can be also written as
\[ P(B \mid A) = \frac{ P(A \mid B) \cdot P(B) }{ P(A \mid B) \cdot P(B) + [1 - P(A^c \mid B^c)] \cdot [1 - P(B)] } \, . \]
Example: Let us revisit the lie detector scenario. Under the assumptions of \(P(D \mid L) = 0.8\), \(P(D \mid L^c) = 0.05\), and \(P(L) = 0.9\). Apply the Bayes’ Theorem (in the form of Equation 1) to find the probability that the suspect is lying given the lie detector claims it is a lie, or \(P(L \mid D)\):

In words, if the lie detector indicated that the suspect lied, there is a ________ probability that the suspect really lied.

1.1 Sensitivity and Specificity
Bayes Theorem is commonly applied to scenarios where we only know the probability of a detection under a particular condition, but we need to know the probability fo the condition given a positive detection.

In the context of the lie detector scenario, the conditional probability \(P(D \mid L)\) is called the sensitivity. A high sensitivity implies a high chance of detecting a lie.
The conditional probability \(P(D^c \mid L^c)\) is called the specificity. A high specificity implies a high chance of detecting a truth.
The probability \(P(L)\) is called the prevalence. A high prevalence implies that subjects lie frequently.
The conditional probability \(P(L \mid D)\) is called the positive predictive value. This is the value that tells us how good the lie detector really is!

Equation 1 informs that the reliability of a lie detector depends on the sensitivity and specificity (how good the lie detector is), but it also depends on the prevalence (how untruthful or truthful subjects are).
Given the sensitivity (\(\texttt{sens}\)) and specificity (\(\texttt{spec}\)), the positive predictive value (\(\texttt{ppv}\)) is a function of the prevalence (\(\texttt{ppv}\)) as follows:
\[\texttt{ppv} = \frac{ \texttt{sens} \cdot \texttt{prev} }{ \texttt{sens} \cdot \texttt{prev} + (1 - \texttt{spec}) \cdot (1 - \texttt{prev}) } \, .\]
The below R code demonstrates the relationship between \(\texttt{ppv}\) and \(\texttt{prev}\) at \(\texttt{sens} = 0.8\) and \(\texttt{spec} = 0.95\). The graph demonstrates that the positive predictive value \(P(B \mid A)\) increases with respect to the prevalence \(P(B)\). In other words, we need frequent lies (i.e., \(P(B)\) is high) in order for the lie detector to predict lies well (i.e., \(P(L \mid D)\) is high).








Notice how the positive predictive values (\(\texttt{ppv}\)) changes based on the prevalence of lies. If the suspect is truthful (low prevalence) how does this affect the ability of the machine to detect a lie?
Let’s observe the positive predictive values across all possible prevalences.

Example: Let us continue from the previous example. If the lie detect is quiet (no indication of a lie), what is the probability that the suspect really did not lie? In other words, what is the conditional probability of \(L^c\) given \(D^c\)? Applying the Bayes’ Theorem.






Such a low probability implies that we cannot trust the suspect when there is no indication of a lie by the lie detector. It is only useful when the lie detector indicates that it is a lie.

Let (C) denote “the condition is present” and (+) denote “the screening test is positive.” Then

\frac{P(+ \mid C)P(C)}
{P(+ \mid C)P(C) + P(+ \mid \neg C)P(\neg C)}.\]

A condition occurs in 1 out of every 2,000 pregnancies. A screening test detects the condition 95% of the time when it is present and has a 1% false-positive rate.
If a patient receives a positive result, what is the probability that the fetus actually has the condition?

The test identifies \((0.95(100) = 95)\) true positives.
Of the 199,900 pregnancies without the condition, \(1%\) produce false positives: \((0.01(199,900) = 1,999)\).

Test A screens for Condition A, which occurs in 1 in 100 pregnancies. Test B screens for Condition B, which occurs in 1 in 2,000 pregnancies. Both tests have 99% sensitivity and a 1% false-positive rate.
For each test, calculate \(P(\text{condition} \mid \text{positive test})\). Why can equally accurate tests lead to very different interpretations of a positive result?






TipComparing Two Conditions

So a positive test gives a 50% probability that Condition A is present.
For Condition B:
\[\frac{(.99)(.0005)}{(.99)(.0005) + (.01)(.9995)} \approx 0.0472.\]
So a positive test gives only about a 4.72% probability that Condition B is present. The key difference is the prevalence: Condition B is much rarer.

\[\frac{(.95)(.004)}{(.95)(.004) + (.01)(.996)} \approx 0.276.\]
The probability after a positive result is about 27.6%. The test’s sensitivity and false-positive rate stayed the same; the prior probability (prevalence) increased.





1.2.6 A Negative Result
A condition occurs in 1 in 500 pregnancies. A screening test has 98% sensitivity and a 2% false-positive rate.
If the result is negative, what is the probability that the fetus still has the condition?






TipA Negative Result Solution





The false-negative rate is \[(1 - .98 = .02)\]. Therefore,
\[P(C \mid -) = \frac{(.02)(.002)}{(.02)(.002) + (.98)(.998)} \approx 0.0000409.\]
The probability is approximately 0.0041%, or about 1 in 24,450.





1.2.7 An Advertising Claim
A company advertises that its screening test is “99% accurate.” Suppose the condition occurs in 1 in 10,000 pregnancies, sensitivity is 99%, and specificity is 99%.

Find the positive predictive value.

Is “99% accurate” enough information to tell a patient the chance that a positive result is correct? Explain using Bayes’ theorem.







TipAn Advertising Claim Solution





\[P(C \mid +) = \frac{(.99)(.0001)}{(.99)(.0001) + (.01)(.9999)} \approx 0.0098.\]
The positive predictive value is about 0.98%.
No: a general accuracy claim omits the condition’s prevalence, as well as the separate sensitivity and specificity values that Bayes’ theorem requires.





1.2.8 A Follow-up Diagnostic Test
A screening test yields a 4% probability that a fetus has a condition after a positive result. A follow-up diagnostic test has 99.9% sensitivity and 99.9% specificity.
Assuming the diagnostic test is positive, use Bayes’ theorem to estimate the updated probability that the fetus has the condition. Explain why follow-up testing matters.






TipA Follow-up Diagnostic Test Solution





Treat the 4% result as the new prior probability, or \(P(C)\):
\[P(C \mid +) = \frac{(.999)(.04)}{(.999)(.04) + (.001)(.96)} \approx 0.9765.\]
The updated probability is approximately 97.65%. A highly accurate follow-up test can substantially reduce uncertainty after a screening result.

The problems are based on the general distinction between prenatal screening and diagnostic testing discussed in the referenced New York Times article. For current clinical guidance, consult a qualified health-care professional.

2 Bayes Theorem and Machine Learning
Bayes Theorem not only spurred a whole new philosophical approach towards statistical inference (called Bayesian Inference), in contrast to the Frequentist Inference approach we will focus on in our course, but it has also provided the foundation for many machine learning methods.

2.1 Example 1: A Naive Bayes Spam Classifier
A Naive Bayes classifier uses Bayes’ theorem to estimate the probability that a message belongs to a class, such as spam or not spam, after observing its words. The word naive refers to an assumption: once the class is known, the model treats the observed word features as independent.
Suppose that, in a training set:

20% of emails are spam: \((P(S) = 0.20)\);
75% of spam emails contain the word “winner”: \((P(W \mid S) = 0.75)\);
5% of non-spam emails contain “winner”: \((P(W \mid \neg S) = 0.05)\).

For an email that contains “winner,” the classifier calculates
\[P(S \mid W) = \frac{P(W \mid S)P(S)} {P(W \mid S)P(S) + P(W \mid \neg S)P(\neg S)}.\]
\[P(S \mid W) = \frac{(.75)(.20)}{(.75)(.20) + (.05)(.80)} = \frac{.15}{.19} \approx 0.789.\]
So the model estimates a 78.9% probability that the email is spam. In practice, it combines evidence from many words:
\[P(S \mid w_1, \ldots, w_n) \propto P(S)\prod_{i=1}^{n}P(w_i \mid S).\]
The class with the larger posterior probability is the prediction. This is the same update as in the screening problems: begin with a prior probability, then revise it using evidence.


2.2 Example 2: Bayesian A/B testing
A/B testing is used to identify the best versions/features to include on apps, websites, and other user interfaces. In a Bayesian A/B test, we have version A and version B, and we treat each version’s conversion rate (getting the user to click on something) as an unknown probability and update our beliefs as observations arrive. Unlike a classical A/B test, the central result can be stated directly as a probability about the two versions.
Suppose a website runs two versions of a sign-up page. Before collecting data, use a uniform prior for each conversion rate, that is both versions have the same probability of working.

The posterior means, \(E\) or expected value, are
\[E[p_A \mid \text{data}] = \frac{13}{102} \approx 12.7%\] and \[E[p_B \mid \text{data}] = \frac{19}{102} \approx 18.6%. \]
To make a decision, draw many samples from the two posterior distributions and count how often \(p_B > p_A\). That fraction estimates \(P(p_B > p_A \mid \text{data})\): the probability, given the model and observed data, that Version B has the higher conversion rate. This illustrates Bayes’ theorem as a learning process—prior beliefs are updated to posterior beliefs as data accumulate.

1 Sample Space
In an experiment, and the set of all outcomes under consideration is referred to as the sample space.
Example: When we toss a coin, the sample space is \(\Omega = \{ h, t \}\) where \(h\) denotes an outcome of head and \(t\) denotes an outcome of tail.
Example: In a random experiment* of tossing a six-sided die, the sample space is \(\Omega = \{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 \}\), the set of six possible outcomes.
Example: In a random experiment* of tossing a pair of six-sided dice, the sample space is \(\Omega = \{ (1, 1), (1, 2), \dots, (6, 6) \}\), the set of 36 possible paired outcomes.






NoteDefinition of Experiment



We will see the term “experiment” used in two different ways in this course. In the context of probability theory, experiment refers to the probability process by which data is generated. Once we learn more about the practice of statistics, experiment refers to a data collection method in which an individual is randomly assigned to a treatment group.

2 Probability Model
Given a sample space \(\Omega\), a probability model is a function \(P\): \(\Omega \rightarrow \mathcal{R}\) which satisfies the two conditions:

\(P(s) \ge 0\) for any \(s \in \Omega\) .
\(\sum_{ s \in \Omega } P(s) = 1\).

Example: Given \(\Omega = \{ h, t \}\) for tossing a coin, assume \(P(h) = 0.8\) and \(P(t) = 0.2\). It is a valid probability model because \(P(h) \ge 0\) and \(P(t) \ge 0\), and
\[\sum_{ s \in \Omega } P(s) = P(t) + P(h) = 0.8 + 0.2 = 1 \, .\]
In this case, we say that “the probability of \(h\) is 0.8” and “the probability of \(t\) is 0.2.” Remember that a probability model is a function which satisfies the two conditions, and the probability of an outcome is a number between zero and one which quantifies the likelihood of the outcome.
Example: Given \(\Omega = \{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 \}\) for tossing a six-sided die, assume all six outcomes are equally likely. The probability model which expresses this assumption can be written as \(P(s) = \frac{1}{6}\) for \(s = 1, 2, \dots, 6\). This probability model can be graphically represented as follows.

3 Event
Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space. An event is a subset of \(\Omega\).
Example: Given \(\Omega = \{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 \}\) for tossing a six-sided die, \(O = \{ 1, 3, 5 \}\) and \(E = \{ 2, 4, 6 \}\) are events because \(O \subseteq \Omega\) and \(E \subseteq \Omega\) . If any outcome in an event occurred, we say that the event occurred. For example, if we toss a six-sided die and an outcome of 1 occurred, we say that the event \(O\) occurred.
The probability of \(O\) is calculated as follows:
\[P(O) = P(1) + P(3) + P(5) = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} = 0.5 \, .\]
Similarly, the probability of \(E\) is \(P(E) = 0.5\). Why?
What do you notice about the relationship between \(O\) and \(E\) as they relate to the sample space?
At the end of semester, suppose students earn one of the following letter grades: \(\Omega = \{ a, b, c, d, f \}\). Historically, 15%, 20%, 30%, 20%, and 15% of students earned \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(d\), and \(f\), respectively. The following probability model reflects this history: \(P(a) = P(f) = 0.15\), \(P(b) = P(d) = 0.2\), and \(P(c) = 0.3\). It can be graphically expressed as follows.








Let \(G\) be the event of passing this course by earning \(a\), \(b\), or \(c\). The probability of \(G = \{ a, b, c \}\) is
\[P(G) = P(a) + P(b) + P(c) = 0.15 + 0.2 + 0.3 = 0.65 \, .\] Let \(G^c\) be the event of not passing this course. In this case, \(G^c = \{ d, f \}\), and we \(G^c\) is called the complementary of \(G\). We can calculate the probability of \(G^c\) as
\[ P(G^c) = P(d) + P(f) = 0.2 + 0.15 = 0.35 \, . \]
Alternatively,
\[P(G^c) = 1 - P(G) = 1 - 0.65 = 0.35 \, .\]
Note: By convention, \(P( \emptyset ) = 0\) where \(\emptyset\) is the empty set. In words, the probability of no outcomes is zero.

Definition: If two events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent then \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\). In other words, \(A\) and \(B\) are independent when the probability of \(B\) does not change the probability of \(A\).
Definition: We say two events \(A\) and \(B\) are dependent when \(P(A \cap B) \ne P(A)P(B)\). In other words, \(A\) and \(B\) are dependent when the condition of \(B\) changes the probability of \(A\).

1.3 R Coding
R, at its most basic, can be thought of as the most powerful calculator you’ve ever had. R isn’t powerful just from its calculation ability, but its ability to utilize functions to apply complex mathematical operations to whole sets of data, which is what we’re going to learn.
Let’s take a closer look at R commands. Complete the following primer: RStudio Primer: Programming Basics (25 min). (One additional note: the chapter gives some indication of the rules around object names, but doesn’t include one last rule: object names can’t have spaces!

1.3.1 Loading Packages
R comes with what is called a “Base” package, which contains numerous functions. There are tens of thousands of additional packages that contain even more packages for everything from 3-D visualizations to machine learning algorithms. To use functions from other packages you must first install the package

install.packages(c("ggformula", "mosaic", "tidyverse"))

Installation only needs to happen once. If you are using the CSUMB Cal ICOR Server then the above packages are already installed and do not need to be installed again.
Loading packages must happen each session. We should always load our packages first thing. Go ahead and run the following code to load our needed packages.










1.3.2 R Syntax
As you covered in class, the R language has its own set of grammatical rules. The good news is that once you’ve learned the basic R structure, it is easy to apply to new commands.
To get R (or any software) to do anything, there are two important questions you must be able to answer: 1) What do you want R to do, and 2) What must R know to do that?
The answers to those questions can help us fill in the boxes of our generic formula template:



Figure 1: Generic Goal Template


Q. What do you want R to do?
A. goal

This determines the function to use.
Functions carry out commands from their inputs and create an output; in other words, we apply a function to its inputs to create the output.
For a plot, the function will describe what sorts of marks to draw (points, in our example). A function could also describe the type of calculation or descriptive statistic.

Q. What must R know to do that?
A. arguments

The inputs in R are called arguments.
For a plot or statistic calculation, we must identify the variables and the data frame that contains them.

The application of a function to arguments follows a simple structure: the name of a function is followed by a pair of parentheses. Values for the arguments are specified inside the parentheses. If there is more than one argument, the arguments are always separated by a comma.
In the generic function above, goal is the name of any function. The arguments (formula & mydata) identify the variables and dataframe that contains them. The ... indicates any additional arguments we many want to include.
Generally, functions are written as the name of the function followed by parentheses, e.g. log(). The empty parentheses are merely a reminder that the name refers to a function.
Sometimes, functions need more than one argument. R functions require the first argument supplied to them to be something specific, but then arguments can be added as needed – those additional arguments need to be named so that R knows exactly what you are trying to specify. Named arguments always have the form:



Figure 2: Generic Argument Syntax


Those arguments are added as needed in place of the ... in our template (Fig 3). We can include as many arguments as needed as long as we separate each one with a comma.



Figure 3: Adding Arguments into Functions Syntax



1.3.2.1 Formula Template
The formula argument in our template is where we define the variable of data to which we want to apply our goal. There are actually a few options for what that variable can look like, depending on the variables we wish to use. We use y to designate our y-axis variable, x to designate our x-axis variable (or in the second case, one single variable), and z to designate a conditioning variable that lets us create separate panels when we group data. The |z can also be applied to the single variable ~x.



Figure 1: Generic Goal Template




1.3.2.2 Assembling the pieces
Now we need to put together the pieces we’ve learned with our actual scenario. For example, we might keep a record of the number of hours spent studying on each day of the week during week 1 and during week 2 of the semester. We want to make a graphic of the hours spent studying on each day of the week. In this case, we have two variables: hours and day, so we’ll use the template:



Figure 4: All Possible Generic Function Syntax

Learning any new software can feel daunting, but referring back to this template and asking yourself the two questions – what do I want R to do? what must R know to do that? – will help you throughout your time working with R.



1.3.3 Vectors, Objects, & Dataframes
The real power of R comes not from calculating values like a calculator, but in manipulating sets of data. Vectors are sets of data that are organized together. Groups of vectors that are associated are dataframes.
For example, we could load a version of our data on hours spent studying in week 1 and week 2 that has three columns, one for day and one for each week.

To be able to work with the dataframe in R, we need to read the csv file into R, using read_csv() which comes from the tidyverse package. We apply that function to the name of the csv file we wish to load, inside quotation marks. Go ahead and run the following code.














WarningError: could not find function "read_csv"





If you get the error could not find function "read_csv" be sure you ran the code in Section 1.3.1.



That is okay, but that code alone means that R reads it and then immediately forgets it. If you tried this, your data wouldn’t appear in your “Environment” pane. We need R to remember and store the information in its active memory.
We can store information in R to use again later as an object. An object is a name given to a set of information in R. It can hold dataframes, vectors, numbers, or outputs from commands. To store information, we have to use an assignment operator, <-. Anything on the right of the assignment operator is stored as the name on the left of the assignment operators.



Figure 5: Generic Stored Object and Assignment Syntax*


Names of objects in R can be almost anything, as long as it doesn’t start with a number, doesn’t contain a mathematical operator (*, /, ^, etc.) and doesn’t contain a space. It is also good practice not to name objects the same as function names.
Thus, my code now becomes the following (run it and see what happens!).

Figure 6: Environment Pane


We can look at all the data within these vectors again by typing the object name into the line of code without any other function. Doing so will print the dataframe to your screen as an output. Go ahead and run the code.








Sometimes we don’t want to see all the data, as there are hundreds of data points. We may just want to see the first few lines of data to get a feel for how it is entered. In that case, we can use the function head() to see the first 6 lines of cases:








Our vectors are embedded within an object. To access them, we need to direct R first to the dataframe object, then to the variable object. We do so using one of two structures, depending on the function. We also need to know the names our variables are called. We can find out the names our variables are called by using the code names()








The first you have already seen in our template – we identify the dataframe using an argument. We can then apply functions to specific variables within our dataframe, such as finding the mean number of hours studied in week 1:

If your data has missing values, or NA, you will need to add na.rm = TRUE as an argument in your code so that the mean, or other goal function calculates the correct values.


or the total number of hours studied across week 1:








Some functions don’t accept the data argument. In those cases, we identify the dataframe and variable using the structure: DATAFRAME$VARIABLE. We can then find the total number of rows in study using the function length()








You will notice that mean() and sum() calculated a single value across the vector. Other functions/operations are vectorized functions - they will apply to each element within the vector and return a vector as the output.
For example, if instead of the total number of hours studied across the week, we wanted to know the total number of hours studied on each day of the week, between weeks. We can’t use sum() because it collapses the information of the days of the week. We can instead add our vectors together:








You will notice that the output of this is to return a vector. Each element of the vector was created by adding the same element of each variable. For example, the first value, 3, was obtained by adding the number of hours studied on Monday of week 1 (1) with the number of hours studied on Monday of week 2 (2), for a total of 3 hours studied on Monday across the two weeks.
A few other useful functions can help us understand the dataset we loaded into R. ncol() lets us determine the number of variables in the dataset. nrow() lets us determine the number of rows (sometimes the same as cases) in the dataset.

Markdown is a way to encode formatting on text in an unobtrusive way (compared to, say, html). Quarto documents use the Markdown language to code the text in the document, and allow you to embed code chunks that execute R code. Your finished .qmd document can be ‘rendered’ to other document types, and the markdown language converts to specific formatting.
Check out the markdown and rendered text side-by-side:

3.1.4 Mathematics
We often want to write small mathematics equations or write mathematical symbols. This is actually much easier in .qmd than in Word.
We surround an equation with $ signs: $e=mc^2$ which will appear as \(e=mc^2\) in the rendered document.
Here are some examples of the type of mathematics you will use within your Quarto documents.

3.1.4.1 Greek Letters
We often want to use statistical symbols within markdown to denote parameters with Greek letters. They are called by using a backslash (\) and then the full name of the Greek letter, such as \alpha, and surrounded by $ to be called within the equation-mode:

We can add labels #| label: to support easy navigation as well, but be careful, DO NOT REPEAT LABELS or this will cause an error when you render the .qmd file.

At the beginning of each Quarto document there should be a special code chunk called the setup chunk. This is where we read the packages used in the rest of the document. We often use #| include: false to as an option in the setup code chunk to hide the output in the rendered document.

3.1.6 In-line code
One of the neat features in Quarto files is the ability to combine code chunks, text, and automatically include (or not– but we always will in this class) code and outputs in the finished document. We’ve been writing code in the code chunks, but you can also write it directly in line with the text using some specific formatting.
Let’s demonstrate with our small study dataset. First, we need to read in the data as an object.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| label: read-study-data
study <- read_csv("study.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) #stops some extra output
```

Then we could calculate the mean:

```{r}
#| label: mean-wk1
mean(~wk1, data = study)
```

By running the code as above, we calculated the mean, but didn’t save it as an object – it just prints to screen and is forgotten by R. If we save the output as an object, we can use it within the Quarto file. When you save an output to an object name, it will not print the value to the screen unless you tell R to provide the value.

```{r}
#| label: mean-wk1-assigned
mwk1 <- mean(~wk1, data = study) # calculates mean and saves it as mwk1
mwk1 # prints to screen the value saved to the object name
```

[1] 1.142857

title: Introduction to Probability Theory II

2 Conditional Probability

2.1 Conditional Probability Based on Data
In basketball, we may consider six outcomes:

missing a free throw (\(s_1\)),

making a free throw (\(s_2\)),

missing a two-pointer (\(s_3\)),

making a two-pointer (\(s_4\)),

missing a three-pointer (\(s_5\)), and

making a three-pointer (\(s_6\)).

Given the sample space \(\Omega = \{ s_1, s_2, s_3, s_4, s_5, s_6 \}\), let

\(A_1 = \{ s_1, s_2 \}\),

\(A_2 = \{ s_3, s_4 \}\),

\(A_3 = \{ s_5, s_6 \}\), and

\(S = \{ s_2, s_4, s_6 \}\).

In words, \(A_1\) is a free throw attempt (whether it was a failure or a success), \(A_2\) is a two-pointer attempt, and \(A_3\) is a three-pointer attempt, \(S\) is a shot made (a free throw, two-pointer, or three-pointer), and \(S^c\) is a shot missed.
Table 1 is the contingency table by the shot type and shot result of Michael Jordan in the 1985 NBA Season. By dividing each cell of Table 1 by the total number of attempts 2,423, Table 2 represents the contingency table in terms of probabilities.

There are two kinds of probability in Table 2.

Joint probability: \(P(A_1 \cap S) = \frac{630}{2423} = 0.260\) means 26.0% of his shots were free throws made, \(P(A_3 \cap S^c) = \frac{43}{2423} = 0.018\) means 1.8% of his shots were three-pointers missed.
Marginal probability: \(P(A_1) = \frac{746}{2423} = 0.308\) means 30.8% of his shots were free throws (whether it made or missed), \(P(S) = \frac{1476}{2423} = 0.609\) means 60.9% of his shots were made (free throws, two-pointers, or three-pointers), and \(P(S^c) = 1 - 0.609 = 0.391\) means 39.1% were missed.

Based on a joint probability and marginal probability, we can calculate a conditional probability. For example,
\[P( S \mid A_1 ) = \frac{ P( S \cap A_1 ) }{ P(A_1) } = \frac{630/2423}{746/2423} = \frac{630}{746} = 0.845 \, .\]
In this case, we say that the conditional probability of \(S\) (success) given \(A_1\) (free throw) is 0.845, and it is interpreted as follows: 84.5% of free throws were successful (630 out of 746 as shown in Table 1). Here is another conditional probability.
\[P( A_1 \mid S ) = \frac{ P( A_1 \cap S ) }{ P(S) } = \frac{630/2423}{1476/2423} = \frac{630}{1476} = 0.427 \, .\]
In this case, we say that the conditional probability of \(A_1\) given \(S\) is 0.427, and it is interpreted as follows: 42.7% of shots he made were free throws (639 out of 1476 as shown in Table 1).
Definition: For arbitrary events \(A\) and \(B\), the conditional probability of \(A\) given \(B\) is defined as
\[P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\]
provided that \(P(B) > 0\) (i.e., \(B\) is a possible condition), and the conditional probability of \(B\) given \(A\) is defined as
\[P(B \mid A) = \frac{ P( B \cap A ) }{ P(A) }\]
provided that \(P(A) > 0\).
In practice, conditional probabilities can be calculated when count data are organized by a contingency table like in Table 1 or Table 2. In general, \(P(A \mid B) \ne P(B \mid A)\).


2.2 Conditional Probability Based on Probability Model
Let \(h\) and \(t\) denote head and tail, respectively, for a coin toss. Suppose a coin is tossed three times. The sample space is given by \(\Omega = \{ hhh, hht, hth, htt, thh, tht, tth, ttt \}\). Assume all eight outcomes are equally likely so that the probability of each outcome is \(\frac{1}{8}\). Suppose we need two or more heads to win, and this event can be written as \(W = \{ hhh, hht, hth, thh \}\). Before tossing a coin, the probability of \(W\) is
\[\begin{aligned}
P(W) & = P( \{ hhh, hht, hth, thh \} ) \\
& = P(hhh) + P(hht) + P(hth) + P(thh) \\
& = 0.125 + 0.125 + 0.125 + 0.125 \\
& = 0.5 \, .
\end{aligned}\]
Suppose \(h\) occurred for the first toss. Given this outcome, what is the probability of winning? The condition (\(h\) for the first toss) can be written as \(H_1 = \{ hhh, hht, hth, htt \}\). By the definition of conditional probability,
\[\begin{aligned}
P( W \mid H_1 ) & = \frac{ P( W \cap H_1 ) }{ P(H_1) } = \frac{ P( \{ hhh, hht, hth \} ) }{ P( \{ hhh, hht, hth, htt \} ) } = \frac{ 3/8 }{ 4/8 } = 0.75 \, . \notag
\end{aligned}\]


2.3 Independence and Conditional Probability
Now we can define Independent Events using conditional probability.
Definition: We say two events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent when \(P(A \mid B) = P(A)\). In other words, \(A\) and \(B\) are independent when the condition of \(B\) does not change the probability of \(A\).
Definition: We say two events \(A\) and \(B\) are dependent when \(P(A \mid B) \ne P(A)\). In other words, \(A\) and \(B\) are dependent when the condition of \(B\) changes the probability of \(A\).
Example: Suppose \(t\) occurred for the second toss after \(h\) occurs on the first toss. Given \(T_2 = \{ hth, htt \}\), the conditional probability of \(W\) is
\[\begin{aligned}
P( W \mid T_2 ) & = \frac{ P( W \cap T_2 ) }{ P(T_2) } = \frac{ P( \{ hth \} ) }{ P( \{ hth, htt \} ) } = \frac{ 1/8 }{ 2/8 } = 0.5 \, . \notag
\end{aligned}\]
As such, the probability of winning has changed as follows: \(P(W) = 0.5\) prior to the first toss, \(P(W \mid H_1) = 0.75\) after observing \(h\) in the first toss, and \(P(W \mid T_2) = 0.5\) after observing \(t\) in the second toss.
Are \(W\) and \(T_2\) dependent or independent?
The new conditional definition of Independence is the best way to determine if two events are independent, but it it is good to remember that if two events are independent then \(P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)\).
Let’s write a short proof:






NoteStep 1





Let \(A\) and \(B\) be independent events.
Then we know that \(P(A \mid B) = P(A)\)









NoteStep 2





By definition of conditional probability we know that
\[P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\]









NoteStep 3





Therefore,
\[P(A) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}\]
So,
\[P(A)P(B) = P(A \cap B)\]

4 Law of Total Probability
As \(D\), \(R\), and \(I\) are a partition of \(\Omega\), the probability of \(G\) is the sum of the three joint probabilities as follows:
\[\begin{aligned}
P(G) & = P(G \cap D) + P(G \cap R) + P(G \cap I) \\
& = 0.45 + 0.01 + 0.02 \\
& = 0.48 \, .
\end{aligned}\]
Theorem: Suppose \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_m\) are a partition of the sample space \(\Omega\). For any event \(B\) (a subset of \(\Omega\)),
\[P(B) = P(B \cap A_1) + P(B \cap A_2) + \dots + P(B \cap A_m) \, . \]
It is known as the Law of Total Probability (or simply LTP).

title: Introduction to Probability Theory II
text:
5 Multiplication Rule
Recall that the conditional probability of an \(A\) given \(B\) is defined as
\[P(A \mid B) = \frac{ P(A \cap B) }{ P(B) }\]
provided that \(P(B) > 0\). Therefore, the joint probability of \(A\) and \(B\) can be written as
\[P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B) \cdot P(B)\]
This rule is known as the Multiplication Rule (or simply MR).
Note: Another expression of the MR is \(P(A \cap B) = P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A)\).

title: Introduction to Probability Theory II
text:
6 Weighted Average of Conditional Probabilities
In the previous example, 48 out of 100 Senators voted guilty, and it can be expressed as \(P(G) = 0.48\). Since \(D\), \(R\), and \(I\) are a partition of the entire sample space, we can express the marginal probability of \(G\) as follows:
\[\begin{aligned}
P(G) & = P(G \cap D) + P(G \cap R) + P(G \cap I) \\
& = P(G \mid D) \cdot P(D) + P(G \mid R) \cdot P(R) + P(G \mid I) \cdot P(I) \\
& = \frac{45}{45} \cdot \frac{45}{100} + \frac{1}{53} \cdot \frac{53}{100} + \frac{2}{2} \cdot \frac{2}{100} \\
& = 1(0.45) + 0.0189(0.53) + 1(0.02) \\
& = 0.48 \, .
\end{aligned}\]
The first equality is by the LTP, and the second equality is by the MR. In other words, the marginal probability \(P(G)\) is the weighted average of \(P(G \mid D)\), \(P(G \mid R)\), and \(P(G \mid I)\) where the conditional probabilities are weighted \(P(D)\), \(P(R)\), and \(P(I)\), respectively. Despite all Democratic and Independent Senators voted for guilty (i.e., \(P(G \mid D) = 1\) and \(P(G \mid I) = 1\)), their parties were not big enough to be the majority (i.e., \(P(D)\) and \(P(I)\) were too small).
Theorem: Suppose \(A_1, A_2, \dots, A_m\) are a partition of the sample space \(\Omega\). For any event \(B\) (a subset of \(\Omega\)), its marginal probability is given by
\[P(B) = P(B \mid A_1) \cdot P(A_1) + P(B \mid A_2) \cdot P(A_2) + \dots + P(B \mid A_m) \cdot P(A_m) \, . \]
In words, the marginal probability of an event is the weighted average of conditional probabilities weighted by the probabilities of the conditions, as long as the conditions are a partition of the entire sample space.
Note: For any event \(A\), the event \(A\) and its complement \(A^c\) are a partition of \(\Omega\). Therefore,
\[P(B) = P(B \mid A) \cdot P(A) + P(B \mid A^c) \cdot P(A^c) \, . \]

title: Discrete Random Variables
text:
1 Discrete Random Variable
Definition: Let \(\Omega\) be a sample space. A real-valued function \(W\): \(\Omega \rightarrow \mathcal{R}\) is called a random variable.
This definition sounds daunting, but we use it everyday.
Example: In an academic transcript, each letter grade in \(\Omega = \{ a, b, c, d, f \}\) is mapped to a numeric value 4, 3, 2, 1, and 0, respectively. This process can be expressed as follows: \(W(a) = 4\), \(W(b) = 3\), \(W(c) = 2\), \(W(d) = 1\), and \(W(f) = 0\). By the aforementioned definition,

\(W\) is a random variable, and
\(\mathcal{S}_W = \{ 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 \}\), the set of possible values of \(W\), is called the support of \(W\)

More specifically, \(W\) is a discrete random variable as its support \(\mathcal{S}_W\) is countable.
Example: At the end of a soccer match, the sample space is \(\Omega = \{ win, tie, loss \}\) for each team. In a professional soccer league, each game outcome is transformed to a numeric score as follows: \(X(win) = 3\), \(X(tie) = 1\), and \(X(loss) = 0\). In this case,

\(X\) is a discrete random variable, and

\(\mathcal{S}_X = \{ 0, 1, 3 \}\) is the support of \(X\).
Each team in a league plays a large number of matches, and this random variable helps ranking teams at the end of the league (e.g., 10 wins, 5 ties, and 5 losses are equivalent to 35 points).
Sometimes, an experiment returns a numeric outcome.
Example: Let \(Y\) be the total number of goals a team scored in a match. In this case,

\(Y\) is a discrete random variable, and
its support is \(\mathcal{S}_Y = \{ 0, 1, 2, 3, \dots \}\).

Let \(Z\) be the outcome of tossing a 6-sided die. In this case, \(Z\) is also a random variable, and its support is \(\mathcal{S}_Z = \{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 \}\).

title: Discrete Random Variables
text:
2 Probability Mass Function
Definition: Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable and \(\mathcal{S}_X\) be its support. We say \(f_X\): \(\mathcal{S}_X \rightarrow \mathcal{R}\) is a probability mass function (or PMF) if it satisfies the following two conditions:

\(f_X(x) \ge 0\) for any \(x \in \mathcal{S}_X\)
\(\sum_{x \in \mathcal{S}_X} f_X(x) = 1\)

We already have seen this kind of definition in a previous lecture. The PMF is a probability model for a discrete random variable.
Example: Let \(X\) be the points earned per match (3 for a win, 1 for a tie, and 0 for a loss). Given the support \(\mathcal{S}_X = \{ 0, 1, 3 \}\), assume the following PMF:
\[f_X(0) = 0.2 \, , \,\,\, f_X(1) = 0.3 \, , \,\,\, f_X(3) = 0.5 \, .\]
It represents that the probability of earning 0 points (a loss) is 0.2, the probability of earning 1 point (a tie) is 0.3, and the probability of earning 3 points (a win) is 0.5. (The probability of earning 2 points is zero in this system.) This probability model can be graphically represented as follows.








Example: Let \(Z\) be the outcome of tossing a 6-sided die. Given its support \(\mathcal{S}_Z = \{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 \}\), assume \(f_Z(1) = f_Z(2) = \dots = f_Z(6)\). In other words, \(f_Z\) expresses that all of the six outcomes are equally likely, and it implies \(f_Z(z) = \frac{1}{6}\) for \(z = 1, 2, \dots, 6\). In this case, we say \(Z\) follows a discrete uniform distribution from 1 to 6, and it can be graphically represented as follows.

title: Discrete Random Variables
text:
3 Expectation
Definition: Let \(X\) be a random variable, \(\mathcal{S}_X\) be the support of \(X\), and \(f_X\) be the PMF of \(X\). The expectation of \(X\) is defined as
\[E(X) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{S}_X} x \cdot f_X(x) \, .\]
The expectation of \(X\) is also called the average, mean, or expected value of \(X\).
Note: In words, the expectation of \(X\) is the weighted average of all possible values of \(X\) where each possible value of \(X\) is weighted by its probability.
Example: In a previous example, we let \(X\) be the points a soccer team earned per match, and assumed \(f_X(0) = 0.2\), \(f_X(1) = 0.3\), and \(f_X(3) = 0.5\). According to the definition, the expectation of \(X\) (i.e., the expected points per match) is






NoteAnswer





\[E(X) = 0 \cdot 0.2 + 1 \cdot 0.3 + 3 \cdot 0.5 = 1.8 \, .\]



Example: Assume we have a new team where \(f_X(0) = 0.5\), \(f_X(1) = 0.1\), and \(f_X(3) = 0.4\). In this case, the expected points per game is






NoteAnswer





\[ E(X) = 0 \cdot 0.5 + 1 \cdot 0.1 + 3 \cdot 0.4 = 1.3 \, . \]



Which team is is better on average when it comes to points per game?






NoteAnswer





The former team is better than the latter team by 0.5 points on average.



Example: In the example of tossing a six-sided die, we assumed \(f_Z(z) = \frac{1}{6}\) for \(z = 1, 2, \dots, 6\). By the definition, the expected outcome is






NoteAnswer





\[\begin{aligned}
E(Z) & = \sum_{z = 1}^6 s \cdot f_Z(z) \\
& = \sum_{z = 1}^6 z \cdot \frac{1}{6} \\
& = \frac{1}{6} \cdot \sum_{z = 1}^6 z \\
& = \frac{1}{6} \cdot (1 + 2 + \dots + 6) \\
& = 3.5 \, .
\end{aligned}\]

title: Discrete Random Variables
text:
4 Variance
In some sense, the expectation characterizes a probability model in terms of the central tendency. We can also characterize a probability model in terms of variability or dispersion from the expectation.
Definition: Let \(X\) be a random variable, \(\mathcal{S}_X\) be the support of \(X\), and \(f_X\) be the PMF of \(X\). Let \(E(X)\) be the expectation of \(X\). The variance of \(X\) is defined as
\[ V(X) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{S}_X} [x - E(X)]^2 \cdot f_X(x) \, . \]
In words, the variance is the expected square distance of \(X\) from \(E(X)\), and it quantifies the variability of the random variable \(X\) from its own average \(E(X)\).
Example: In the soccer example, given the PMF \(f_X(0) = 0.2\), \(f_X(1) = 0.3\), and \(f_X(3) = 0.5\), we calculated the expectation, \(E(X) = 1.8\), and we can calculate that the variance as follows:






Note





\[ V(X) = (0 - 1.8)^2 \cdot 0.2 + (1 - 1.8)^2 \cdot 0.3 + (3 - 1.8)^2 \cdot 0.5 = 1.56 \, . \]



Given the other PMF \(f_X(0) = 0.5\), \(f_X(1) = 0.1\), and \(f_X(3) = 0.4\). we calculated that the expectation is \(E(X) = 1.3\), and we can calculate that the variance is \(V(X) = 2.01\). The latter team has the lower expected points per game, and it has a higher variance than the former team.
Definition: The standard deviation of \(X\) is defined as \(\sqrt{ V(X) }\), the square root of the variance of \(X\).
Example: In the example of tossing a six-sided die, we assumed \(f_Z(z) = \frac{1}{6}\) for \(z = 1, 2, \dots, 6\), and we calculated \(E(Z) = 3.5\). By the definition of variance,






Note





\[\begin{aligned}
V(Z) & = \sum_{z = 1}^6 [z - E(Z)]^2 \cdot f_Z(z) \\
& = \sum_{s = 1}^6 [z - 3.5]^2 \cdot \frac{1}{6} \\
& = \frac{1}{6} \cdot \sum_{z = 1}^6 [z - 3.5]^2 \\
& = \frac{1}{6} \cdot [ (1 - 3.5)^2 + (2-3.5)^2 + \dots + (6 - 3.5)^2 ] \\
& = 2.9167 \, ,
\end{aligned}\]



and the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{V(Z)} = 1.7078\).

title: Discrete Random Variables
text:
5 Bernoulli Random Variable
When an experiment has binary outcomes, say 0 and 1, it is called a Bernoulli experiment. A traditional example is a coin toss. Let \(X\) be the outcome of a coin toss where \(X = 1\) represents an outcome of head and \(X = 0\) represents an outcome of tail, so the support is \(\mathcal{S}_X = \{ 0, 1 \}\). In this case, we say \(X\) is a Bernoulli random variable, and its PMF is generically expressed by \(f_X(1) = \theta\) and \(f_X(0) = 1 - \theta\) where \(\theta\) is a fixed number between 0 and 1. In this case, \(\theta\) implies the probability of head, and \(1 - \theta\) implies the probability of tail.
In this generic expression, the expectation of \(X\) is






Note





\[E(X) = 0 \cdot (1-\theta) + 1 \cdot \theta = \theta \, ,\]



and the variance of \(X\) is






Note





\[\begin{aligned}
V(X) & = (0 - \theta)^2 \cdot (1-\theta) + (1 - \theta)^2 \cdot \theta \\
& = \theta^2 \cdot (1-\theta) + (1-\theta)^2 \cdot \theta \\
& = \theta \cdot (1-\theta) \cdot [\theta + (1-\theta)] \\
& = \theta \cdot (1-\theta) \, .
\end{aligned}\]



Example If we assume that the probability of head is \(\theta = 0.51\) for a Bernoulli random variable \(X\), find the expectation and variance.






Note





\(E(X) = 0.51\) and a variance of \(V(X) = 0.51 \cdot (1-0.51) = 0.2499\).

title: Discrete Random Variables
text:
6 Binomial Random Variable
Let \(X\) be a Bernoulli random variable. Let \(X = 1\) be a success and \(X = 0\) be a failure. Let \(\theta\) be the probability of \(X = 1\). Assume the Bernoulli experiment is repeated \(n\) times under the same condition. More specifically, assume the following:

\(n\) is fixed.
\(\theta\) is constant.
Outcomes of \(n\) trials are independent.

Let \(Y\) be the number of successes in \(n\) trials. In this case, \(Y\) is called the binomial random variable, the support is \(\mathcal{S}_Y = \{ 0, 1, 2, \dots, n \}\), and the PMF of \(Y\) is given by
\[f_Y(y) = \frac{n!}{y! (n-y)!} \, \theta^y \, (1-\theta)^{n-y} \, , \,\,\, y = 0, 1, 2, \dots, n \, .\]
In this case, we simply write \(Y \sim \mathrm{Bino}(n, \theta)\).
Example: Suppose we toss a coin three times where the probability of a head is \(\theta = 0.9\) for each trial. Let \(Y\) be the number of heads out of \(n = 3\). Assuming \(Y \sim \mathrm{Bino}(3, 0.9)\), which implies the three assumptions are satisfied, the support is \(\mathcal{S}_Y = \{ 0, 1, 2, 3 \}\), and the PMF is as follows:






Note





\[\begin{aligned}
f_Y(0) & = \frac{3!}{0! \, 3!} \, (0.9)^0 \, (0.1)^{3} = 0.001 \, , \\
f_Y(1) & = \frac{3!}{1! \, 2!} \, (0.9)^1 \, (0.1)^{2} = 0.027 \, , \\
f_Y(2) & = \frac{3!}{2! \, 1!} \, (0.9)^2 \, (0.1)^{1} = 0.243 \, , \\
f_Y(3) & = \frac{3!}{3! \, 0!} \, (0.9)^3 \, (0.1)^{0} = 0.729 \, .
\end{aligned}\]



We can calculate \(f_Y(y)\) by \(\texttt{dbinom}(y, n, \theta)\) in R.








We can graphically show the probability model as follows.








According to the definition, the expected number of heads out of three trials is






Note





\[E(Y) = 0 \cdot 0.001 + 1 \cdot 0.027 + 2 \cdot 0.243 + 3 \cdot 0.729 = 2.7 \, ,\]



and the variance is






Note





\[\begin{aligned}
V(Y) & = (0 - 2.7)^2 \cdot 0.001 + (1 - 2.7)^2 \cdot 0.027 \\
& \,\,\, + (2 - 2.7)^2 \cdot 0.243 + (3 - 2.7)^2 \cdot 0.729 \\
& = 0.27 \, .
\end{aligned}\]



Note: If \(Y \sim \mathrm{Bino}(n, \theta)\), then

\(E(Y) = n \cdot \theta\) and

\(V(Y) = n \cdot \theta(1-\theta)\).

In the previous example, the expectation and variance can be calculated as follows:






Note





\[\begin{aligned}
E(Y) & = 3(0.9) = 2.7 \, , \\
V(Y) & = 3(0.9)(1-0.9) = 0.27 \, .
\end{aligned}\]

       title = "Hotel 3" ) +
  ylim(0, 1)












TipAnswer





\(E(Z) = 3\)
\(V(Z) = 4\)




Why is it important to consider both average and variance when we describe a probability model?







TipAnswer





Both average and variance are numeric descriptions of a probability distribution. The average measures the center of a probability distribution, and the variance measures the variability of an outcome around the center. It is possible that two probability distributions have the same average with different variances like the ratings of Hotels 2 and 3. Even though the two hotels have the same average rating of 3, visitors have extreme experiences in Hotel 3 (which results in a variance of 4), whereas visitors have relatively consistent experiences (near the average) in Hotel 2 (which results in a variance of 1.2).

1 Sampling Distribution of Sample Mean
Definition: We say \((X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)\) is an independent and identically distributed sample (or simply an i.i.d. sample) of size \(n\) if \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n\) are independent (unrelated) random variables and they have the same PMF or PDF.
Definition: The simple average of \(n\) random variables, \(\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\), is called the sample mean, and the probability model for \(\bar{X}\) is called the sampling distribution of the sample mean.
Example: The above definitions are somewhat technical, and here is an example. Assume \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are two independent random variables. In other words, the outcome of \(X_1\) does not affect the outcome of \(X_2\) and vice versa. Further assume that the support of \(X_1\) and of \(X_2\) are \(\{ 0, 1, 3 \}\) and their PMFs are identical as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_X(0) & = 0.2 \, , \\
f_X(1) & = 0.4 \, , \\
f_X(3) & = 0.4 \, .
\end{aligned}
\]
By the definition, \((X_1, X_2)\) is an i.i.d. sample of size \(n = 2\), and let \(\bar{X} = \frac{1}{2} (X_1 + X_2)\) be the sample mean. Table 1 shows all nine possible outcomes of \((X_1, X_2)\), their probabilities, and values of \(\bar{X}\).

\[

f_{\bar{X}}(0.0) & = 0.04 \, , \\

Can you imagine the process of finding the exact sampling distribution of \(\bar{X} = \frac{1}{3} (X_1 + X_2 + X_3)\) for \(n = 3\)? How about \(n = 10\)? When \(n\) is large, finding the exact sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) is very laborious, but we can approximate the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) using simulations as follows:

Step 1: Generate an i.i.d. sample \((X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)\) of size \(n\) given the PMF or PDF.
Step 2: Calculate the sample mean \(\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\).
Step 3: Repeat Steps 1 and 2 many times (say 10,000 times) and store the value of \(\bar{X}\) each time.
Step 4: Visualize the sampling distribution of \(\bar{X}\) using a histogram.

title: Continuous Random Variables
text:
2 Central Limit Theorem
Theorem: Let \((X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n)\) be an i.i.d. sample of size \(n\) from a probability model with a model mean of \(\mu\) and a model standard deviation of \(\sigma\). The approximate sampling distribution of \(\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) follows a normal distribution as \(n\) goes to infinity, more specifically,
\[
\bar{X} \sim \mathrm{N} \left( \mu, \, \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \right)
\]
It is known as the Central Limit Theorem (or CLT).
We can verify the CLT in the previous simulation. We generated an i.i.d. sample of size \(n = 10\) from the following probability model: \(f_X(0) = 0.2\), \(f_X(1) = 0.4\), and \(f_X(3) = 0.4\). The mean, variance, and standard deviation of this model are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
E(X) & = 0 \cdot 0.2 + 1 \cdot 0.4 + 3 \cdot 0.4 = 1.6 \, , \\
V(X) & = (0 - 1.6)^2 \cdot 0.2 + (1 - 1.6)^2 \cdot 0.4 + (3 - 1.6)^2 \cdot 0.4 = 1.44 \, , \\
\sqrt{ V(X) } & = \sqrt{1.44} = 1.2 \, .
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\mu = 1.6\) and \(\sigma = 1.2\), and approximate sampling distribution of \(\bar{X} = \frac{1}{10} (X_1 + X_2 + \dots + X_{10})\) is
\[
\bar{X} \sim \mathrm{N} \left( 1.6, \, \frac{1.2}{\sqrt{10}} \right) \, .
\]
The standard deviation of \(\bar{X}\), \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.2}{\sqrt{10}} = 0.3795\), is called the standard error of \(\bar{X}\), and it quantifies the variability of \(\bar{X}\) around the mean \(\mu = 1.6\).
If we generate an i.i.d. sample of size \(n = 50\), we can guess that the approximate sampling distribution of \(\bar{X} = \frac{1}{50} (X_1 + X_2 + \dots + X_{50})\) will be
\[
\bar{X} \sim \mathrm{N} \left( 1.6, \, \frac{1.2}{\sqrt{50}} \right)
\]
where \(\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1.2}{\sqrt{50}} = 0.1697\) is the standard error of \(\bar{X}\).

title: common-errors
text: One of the most frustrating parts for people learning R is troubleshooting errors. R is incredibly powerful, but it is dumb. It can’t guess what you meant, nor add in a comma that you forgot to type. Read Chapter 6: Deciphering Common R Errors (5 min) which covers the most common errors in R and how to decipher them. R errors aren’t always clear to new users, but they almost always will direct you to where the problem occurs. Sometimes that is just telling you that it can’t find the file or object you are trying to point it to. Other times, it will repeat your code right up to the point where it didn’t understand. That helps focus your attention when searching for errors.

title: RStudio Orientation
text:
Let’s start working in R! 🥳



Introduction to R
R is a statistical programming language. Unlike more general-purpose languages, R is optimized for working with data and doing statistics. R was created by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman in 1993 (hence “R”) and was formally released by the R Core Group in 1997 (a group of 20-ish volunteers who are the only people who can change the base (built-in) functionality of R). If you want to build an independent, standalone graphical interface, or run a web server, R is probably not the ideal language to use (you might want C / Python or PHP / Python, respectively). If you want to vacuum up a bunch of data, fit several regression models, and then compare the models, R is a great option and will be faster than working in a more general-purpose language like C or base Python.
In general, R is…

vector-based
1 indexed (start counting 1, 2, 3, …)
a scripting language (R code does not have to be compiled before it is run)

One thing to know about R is that it is open-source. This means that no company owns R (like there is for SAS or Matlab) and that developers cannot charge for the use of their R software. This does not mean that all of your code needs to be public (you can keep your code private), but it is important to be a good open-source citizen by sharing your code publicly when possible (later we will learn about GitHub), contributing to public projects and packages, creating your own packages, and using R for ethical and respectful projects.

📖 Suggested Reading: Basics of R






NoteThe History of R



If you would like to learn more about the history of R, here is an excellent article written by Roger Peng.




💻 Useful Tutorial: R Programming Basics






NoteProgramming in R



This tutorial gives you an overview of the foundations that make up the R programming language, including:

functions and their arguments
accessing help files
making code comments
object types (e.g., vectors, lists, )
data types (e.g., numeric, integer, double, character)
R’s package system

Exploring the Panes

Includes the text editor. This is where you’ll do most of your work.

The logo on the script file indicates the file type. When an R file is open, there are Run and Source buttons on the top which allow you to run selected lines of code (Run) or source (run) the entire file. Code line numbers are provided on the left (this is a handy way to see where in the code the errors occur), and you can see line:character numbers at the bottom left. At the bottom right, there is another indicator of what type of file Rstudio thinks this is.


In the top right, you’ll find the environment, history, and connections tabs. The environment tab shows you the objects available in R (variables, data files, etc.), the history tab shows you what code you’ve run recently, and the connections tab is useful for setting up database connections.


On the bottom left is the console. There are also other tabs to give you a terminal (command line) prompt, and a jobs tab to monitor progress of long-running jobs. In this class we’ll primarily use the console tab.
